title: Vomiting blood and black stools in a 74-year-old man on ibuprofen and aspirin
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 74-year-old retired sandal maker brought to the ED by ambulance. He has had black, tarry stools for 2 weeks and today vomited blood twice after his usual epigastric pain suddenly got worse. He takes ibuprofen and aspirin. The candidate then interprets his observations, bloods and venous gas and an erect chest X-ray report. They calculate a Glasgow-Blatchford score, give the diagnosis and differentials, outline resuscitation and initial ED management of an upper GI bleed, answer his questions about the cause and his tablets, and set escalation triggers.
focus: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding: recognising a compensated haemorrhage, resuscitating, risk stratifying with the Glasgow-Blatchford score, and starting non-variceal management with early endoscopy
diagnosis: Bleeding peptic ulcer (NSAID and aspirin related)
stem: You are an intern in the Emergency Department of a hospital in the Greater Sydney area. Mr Bruce Birkenstock, a 74-year-old retired sandal maker, has just been brought in by ambulance looking unwell. The paramedics report 2 weeks of black, loose stools and 2 episodes of vomiting blood this morning. He has been placed in a resuscitation-capable bay. A nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from Bruce and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you his observations, his blood results and venous gas, and an erect chest X-ray report. Interpret them, calculate a risk score, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management approach and safety netting, and answer the examiner's questions (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Bruce Birkenstock, a 74-year-old retired sandal maker. You are lying on the trolley, pale and frightened, with a vomit bowl beside you. You are alert and answer clearly, but you are upset about the blood and keep asking whether you will be all right. You are not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Give details only when you are asked. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "Doctor, I've been throwing up blood. I've never seen so much of it. Am I going to be all right?"

The bleeding (give only when asked)

  • Vomiting blood: twice this morning, at about 9 am and again at about 9:45 am, both after the pain got much worse. Each time about a cup to a cup and a half. It was red blood with some clots, not like coffee grounds.
  • You were not retching or vomiting before the blood came up. The blood was the first thing you vomited.
  • Stools: for about 2 weeks your stools have been loose, black and sticky, "like tar", and they smell terrible. About twice a day. You thought it was something you ate.
  • No bright red blood from the back passage before today.

The pain (only when asked)

  • Site: the upper middle of your tummy. It does not go through to your back or up into your chest.
  • Usual pain: a burning, gnawing pain on and off for a few months. It often wakes you at night and eases a bit if you eat something. You put it down to your reflux.
  • Today: at about 8 am it suddenly got much worse. It is now 8 out of 10 and constant.
  • Moving makes it a little worse. Nothing makes it better.

Other symptoms (only when asked about each)

  • You have felt light-headed when standing up this morning. You have not fainted or blacked out.
  • You have been more tired and a bit short of breath walking up the hill to the shops this past week.
  • No chest pain and no palpitations.
  • Otherwise well. No recent illness. No weight loss, your appetite is normal, no trouble swallowing, and you do not feel full early.
  • No yellow skin or eyes, no swelling of your tummy or legs, no easy bruising.
  • No fever.

Past history (only when asked)

  • A stroke in 2013. You made a good recovery and have no lasting problems.
  • Osteoarthritis in both hips and both knees.
  • High blood pressure and high cholesterol. Your GP says your blood pressure usually runs about 150 over 90.
  • Reflux (GORD) for years.
  • You have never had a stomach ulcer, never had a "camera test" (gastroscopy) and have never been tested for a stomach bug (Helicobacter). No known liver disease.
  • No heart failure and no heart attacks.

Medications and allergies (only when asked)

  • Ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for your hips and knees. You have taken it for months. "It's the only thing that lets me walk."
  • Aspirin 100 mg once a day since your stroke.
  • Atorvastatin 20 mg once a day.
  • Esomeprazole 40 mg once a day. You only take it when the heartburn is bad, so you miss most days.
  • Lisinopril 20 mg once a day. You often forget it because you feel fine.
  • No blood thinners (no warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban or dabigatran), no clopidogrel, no steroids, no antidepressants, no herbal medicines.
  • No known allergies.

Family history

  • Nothing relevant that you know of.

Social history (only when asked)

  • You live with your wife. You have two healthy adult children.
  • Retired sandal maker.
  • Alcohol: 2 to 3 standard drinks a day, usually beer, sometimes wine with dinner. You have never had the shakes when you stopped.
  • Never smoked. No recreational drugs. No tattoos or blood transfusions.
  • If asked whether you would accept a blood transfusion: "Yes, whatever I need, Doc."

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Idea: "I thought it was just my reflux playing up."
  • Concern: you are frightened by the amount of blood and worried you might die. You are also worried about your wife, who is on her way in.
  • Expectation: you want someone to stop the bleeding and tell you what is going on.

The nurse and how Bruce changes

  • If the candidate asks for observations, the nurse gives the set listed under Exam findings.
  • If asked for lying and standing (postural) observations, the nurse says: "We haven't done those yet. He's on bed rest for now."
  • If the candidate calls for senior help, the nurse says: "The ED registrar is on her way."
  • If the candidate asks for cannulas and bloods (including a group and crossmatch), the nurse inserts two large-bore cannulas and sends the bloods. The examiner says the results will be given in Part 2.
  • Partway through, the nurse says: "He's just opened his bowels on the pan. A large, loose, black, tarry stool."
  • If the candidate orders fluids, a PPI, nil by mouth or anything else, the nurse confirms she will arrange it, and the examiner says: "Noted. Please cover your management in Part 2." Bruce says he feels "a little less woozy" if a fluid bolus is started, but nothing else changes.
  • If the candidate asks for imaging, an ECG or results, the examiner says they will be given in Part 2.

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: conscious, alert and oriented. Distressed about what has happened. Pale. Weight about 82 kg.
  • Observations: HR 112 regular, BP 110/80, RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C, BGL 6.8 mmol/L.
  • Hands and peripheries: cool hands, CRT 3 seconds. No clubbing, palmar erythema, leuconychia, Dupuytren's contracture or asterixis.
  • Face and eyes: conjunctival pallor. Sclerae not yellow. Mucous membranes dry.
  • Neck: JVP not seen. Carotid pulses normal.
  • Chest wall: a single spider naevus on the left upper chest. No gynaecomastia. No other stigmata of chronic liver disease.
  • Heart: dual heart sounds, no murmur.
  • Lungs: good air entry throughout, no basal crackles.
  • Abdomen, inspection: not distended. No caput medusae, no scars.
  • Abdomen, palpation: soft. Tender in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant, with voluntary guarding there. No rigidity. Liver and spleen not palpable. No masses.
  • Percussion: percussion tenderness in the epigastrium. No shifting dullness.
  • Auscultation: normal bowel sounds.
  • Aorta: normal, not expansile.
  • Rectal examination (give if the candidate says they would perform it, with consent and a chaperone): black, tarry stool staining around the anus. No haemorrhoids or fissures. Normal anal tone. No masses. Black, tarry, foul-smelling melaena on the glove; no fresh red blood.
  • Everything else normal.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self, confirms Bruce's identity, gains consent and offers a chaperone for the rectal examination.

Recognises from the outset that Bruce is unwell and acts early, without waiting until the end of the history: calls for senior help (ED registrar or consultant) and asks the nurse for two large-bore cannulas and bloods, including a group and crossmatch.
check.d: Credit if this happens within the first few minutes, in any order.

check.x: Acknowledges his distress about the bleeding with empathy, uses plain language and explains each step of the examination before doing it.
History
Characterises the bleeding:

kids.x: Haematemesis: started after the pain suddenly worsened this morning; 2 episodes of about 1 to 1.5 cups each; red blood with clots, not coffee grounds
Melaena: loose, black, tarry, foul-smelling stools for 2 weeks, about twice a day
Asks whether retching or forceful vomiting came before the blood (none, which argues against a Mallory-Weiss tear)

check.x: Characterises the pain: burning, gnawing epigastric pain on and off for months, often at night and eased by food, suddenly much worse at 8 am today (8/10, constant), with no radiation to the back or chest.
Asks about symptoms of blood loss: light-headedness on standing, collapse or blackout (none), tiredness and exertional breathlessness, and chest pain or palpitations (none).
check.d: Syncope scores 2 on the Glasgow-Blatchford score. Chest pain would suggest demand ischaemia.

check.x: Takes a medication history that identifies the bleeding risks:

kids.x: Ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for months, for his hips and knees, and aspirin 100 mg daily since his stroke
Esomeprazole 40 mg prescribed but taken only when the heartburn is bad
Asks specifically about anticoagulants, other antiplatelets, steroids and SSRIs (none)

check.x: Screens for liver disease and varices: quantifies his alcohol (2 to 3 standard drinks a day) and asks about known liver disease, jaundice, swelling of the abdomen or legs, and hepatitis risk factors (none).
Screens for malignancy and previous ulcer disease: weight loss, appetite, dysphagia and early satiety (none); previous ulcer, gastroscopy or Helicobacter pylori testing (none).

Takes the rest of the past history and allergies: stroke in 2013 with a good recovery, hip and knee osteoarthritis, hypertension (usually about 150/90; lisinopril 20 mg, often missed), high cholesterol (atorvastatin 20 mg), GORD, no heart failure; no known allergies.
check.d: Score if stroke, hypertension with usual BP, absence of heart failure and allergies are covered.

check.x: Takes the social history: lives with his wife, two healthy adult children, retired sandal maker, non-smoker, no drugs. Asks whether he would accept a blood transfusion if needed (yes).
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thought it was his reflux, is frightened by the blood and worried he might die, and wants the bleeding stopped.
Examination
General inspection: alert and oriented, distressed and pale. Checks the conjunctivae (pallor).
Asks for a full set of vital signs and identifies the tachycardia (HR 112) and a BP of 110/80, which is low for a man whose usual BP is about 150/90.
check.d: Do not require postural observations: resting tachycardia already shows significant volume loss. Credit a candidate who says postural observations are not needed or not safe for this reason.

check.x: Assesses perfusion and volume status: CRT 3 seconds, cool peripheries, JVP not seen, dry mucous membranes.

Looks for stigmata of chronic liver disease in the hands, face, chest and abdomen, including jaundice, gynaecomastia, caput medusae and ascites, and finds only a single spider naevus on the left chest.
Palpates the abdomen gently and looks for peritonism: a soft, non-distended abdomen with epigastric and right upper quadrant tenderness, voluntary guarding and percussion tenderness, and no rigidity.
Completes the abdominal examination: liver and spleen, shifting dullness, the aorta (expansile mass), bowel sounds.
check.d: Score if at least 3 are examined, including the aorta.

check.x: Auscultates the heart (no murmur) and the lung bases (clear).
Asks for a rectal examination with consent and a chaperone, and interprets the findings: melaena on the glove, no fresh blood, no haemorrhoids, fissure or mass.
check.d: Credit a candidate who says the DRE is still indicated, or who says the melaena stool on the bedpan has already confirmed it and they would document a DRE later with a chaperone.

check.x: Interpretation
Recognises rising HR and falling SBP with further melaena as ongoing bleeding with compensated hypovolaemia despite a white-zone chart, needing review now.
check.d: Credit but do not require noting that no urine has been passed yet and an IDC is needed to measure output. Do not credit calling the absent urine output oliguria; he has been in the ED only about 20 minutes.

check.x: Interprets the Hb of 84 g/L against a baseline of 138 as significant blood loss, and states that the first Hb underestimates an acute bleed.
Interprets a urea of 16.8 with a near-normal creatinine as the pattern of an upper GI bleed (digested blood protein), with some prerenal contribution.
Notes normal platelets, INR and albumin (varices unlikely) and the raised lactate.
check.d: Credit but do not require the GGT and lipase comments, or the mild neutrophilia (a stress response to haemorrhage, but with guarding another reason for a low threshold for CT).

check.x: Calculates the Glasgow-Blatchford score (12: urea 4, Hb 6, HR 1, melaena 1) and states that he is high risk and needs admission and inpatient endoscopy.
check.d: Credit 12 or 13 (13 if the repeat SBP of 106 is used). The critical element is recognising a high score that rules out outpatient care.

check.x: Interprets the erect chest X-ray: no free gas under the diaphragm and no pneumomediastinum. States that this does not exclude a perforation, so CT is needed, before gastroscopy, if the guarding persists or worsens.

Gives the most likely diagnosis as a non-variceal upper GI bleed from a peptic ulcer (credit but do not require "probably duodenal"), justified by at least 3 of: ibuprofen and aspirin, poor PPI adherence, months of nocturnal epigastric pain eased by food, haematemesis with 2 weeks of melaena, the fall in Hb and the raised urea.

Gives at least 3 differentials, each with a feature for or against it from this case. Must include variceal bleeding (for: alcohol and a spider naevus; against: normal platelets, INR and albumin) and perforated ulcer (for: guarding; against: no free gas).
check.d: Also credit erosive oesophagitis or gastritis, Mallory-Weiss tear, gastric cancer or Boerhaave syndrome, each with a reason.

check.x: Management

ABCDE with senior help: airway watch with anaesthetics early if further haematemesis or falling GCS; small crystalloid bolus (e.g. 500 mL) and reassess; early red cells (crossmatched or group-specific) if bleeding continues or no response; MTP if unstable.
check.d: Credit but do not require an ECG (and troponin if chest pain or ECG changes) to look for demand ischaemia, and oxygen only if SpO2 falls.

check.x: States a restrictive threshold (Hb below 70 g/L, or below 80 g/L with significant cardiovascular disease such as ischaemic heart disease) or transfusion for ongoing instability, applies it to Bruce (transfuse if not responding to the bolus), and does not transfuse to a normal Hb.
IV PPI, NBM, titrated analgesia and antiemetic; no NSAIDs.
check.d: Doses are not required. Credit but do not require stating no terlipressin, octreotide or tranexamic acid because the bleed is non-variceal, or that terlipressin and antibiotics would be started if variceal bleeding were suspected.

check.x: Stops ibuprofen permanently and withholds lisinopril. Makes an explicit, senior or gastroenterology-discussed decision about aspirin for secondary stroke prevention: either continues it, or withholds it briefly and restarts it as soon as haemostasis is secure (ideally within 3 to 5 days). Does not stop it indefinitely.
check.d: Credit either continuing or briefly withholding aspirin if it is discussed with the team. Do not credit stopping it with no plan to restart.

check.x: Refers to gastroenterology for gastroscopy within 24 hours (sooner if unstable) and asks general surgery to review because of the guarding. Admits him with frequent observations and fluid balance, with HDU or ICU involvement if he becomes unstable.

Explains to Bruce in plain words that he most likely has a bleeding ulcer caused by the anti-inflammatory tablets and aspirin, and that a camera test will find it and usually treat it. Checks his understanding.
Safety netting
Tells Bruce to call the nurse at once for at least 3 of: vomiting blood again, another black or bloody stool, feeling faint or dizzy, worse or spreading tummy pain, chest pain or breathlessness.

Asks the nurses to escalate (a clinical review for any yellow-zone value, a rapid response for any red-zone value) at least 3 of: rising HR, falling BP, further haematemesis or melaena, low urine output, confusion, or a rigid abdomen.

part2.lead: Here are Bruce's observations, his blood results and venous gas, and the erect chest X-ray report.
part2.patient:
Question 4 opens with Bruce's own question. React to the answer:

  • If told the ibuprofen is the likely cause: "But my knees are killing me without it. What am I supposed to take?" Accept it if the candidate offers paracetamol and a GP plan for his arthritis.
  • Then ask: "And the aspirin? My doctor said it stops another stroke." Accept it if the candidate explains that the team will decide on the aspirin with the stomach specialists, and that it is either kept going or paused only briefly and restarted soon.
  • If the candidate uses jargon (peptic ulcer, endoscopy, PPI, Helicobacter), ask: "What does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: On room air. Arrival set at 10:40 and the nurse's repeat set at 11:00, taken before any treatment had run in. No urine passed yet; no IDC in place.
handover.model:
• Examiner note: both sets were taken before any treatment ordered in Part 1 had run in. If the candidate ordered a fluid bolus, tell them it is now running.
  • Read: at 10:40, HR 112, SBP 110, RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air and temperature 36.9 °C are all in the white zone; CRT 3 seconds. At 11:00, HR is 116 and SBP 106 (both still white), RR 19. He has passed a large melaena stool and the nurse is worried. No urine passed yet: he has been in the ED only about 20 minutes, so this is not oliguria; an IDC is needed to measure output.
  • Meaning: a rising tachycardia with a falling SBP and an already narrow pulse pressure (110/80), in a man whose usual BP is about 150/90, means compensated hypovolaemic shock from ongoing bleeding. A white-zone chart does not mean he is safe: older patients compensate until they decompensate suddenly. A worried nurse is an additional criterion for a clinical review.
  • Changes: clinical review now with senior help, resuscitation, crossmatched blood ready, observations at least every 15 to 30 minutes until stable, an IDC, and a rapid response for any red-zone value.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: haematemesis x2 and melaena per ambulance. Pale. Usual BP about 150/90 per GP.
Large loose black tarry stool on bedpan. No urine passed yet. Doctor at bedside.

handover.label: Bloods and venous blood gas
handover.result: Collected 10:50 at cannulation; venous gas at the same time on room air. Sample not haemolysed. Previous results from GP bloods 6 months ago.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 84 g/L (baseline 138), haematocrit 0.26, MCV 84. WCC 10.6 with neutrophils 8.2. Urea 16.8 (baseline 6.2) with creatinine 102 (baseline 88). Platelets 268, INR 1.1, APTT and fibrinogen normal. Bilirubin, ALT, AST, ALP and albumin normal; GGT 74. Lipase normal. Venous gas pH 7.35, bicarbonate 22, lactate 2.6. Group A positive, antibody screen negative.
  • Meaning: a large blood loss, and the true loss is bigger because the Hb has not yet equilibrated. A urea raised out of proportion to creatinine fits an upper GI source (digested blood) with some prerenal effect. No coagulopathy. Normal platelets, INR, albumin and bilirubin make cirrhosis and varices unlikely; the GGT fits his drinking. Normal lipase makes pancreatitis unlikely. A raised lactate means hypoperfusion. Mild neutrophilia (8.2) with a normal total WCC fits a stress response to acute haemorrhage, but with guarding it is another reason to keep a low threshold for CT.
  • Glasgow-Blatchford score: urea 16.8 (4), Hb below 100 in a man (6), SBP 110 (0), HR 100 or more (1), melaena (1), no syncope, liver disease or heart failure: 12 (13 with the repeat SBP of 106). High risk: admit and arrange endoscopy within 24 hours.
  • Changes: Hb 84 is above the numerical threshold, but he has ongoing instability: transfuse if he does not respond promptly to the bolus. Have crossmatched red cells ready. Repeat Hb. Withhold lisinopril. No variceal treatment.

handover.label: Erect chest X-ray
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, erect AP projection (patient sitting upright for 10 minutes before exposure), 11:15. Both hemidiaphragms fully included.

Clinical details: 74-year-old man. Haematemesis and 2 weeks of melaena. Sudden worsening of epigastric pain this morning, epigastric and RUQ tenderness with voluntary guarding. ?Free gas ?Perforation.

Findings:

  • Diaphragm: no free gas beneath either hemidiaphragm. Normal gastric bubble under the left hemidiaphragm. Costophrenic angles clear.
  • Mediastinum: normal contour. No pneumomediastinum. Trachea central.
  • Heart: size within normal limits for an AP projection.
  • Lungs and pleura: clear lungs. No consolidation, pleural effusion or pneumothorax.
  • Soft tissues: no surgical emphysema.
  • Bones: no acute bony abnormality.

Conclusion: no pneumoperitoneum or pneumomediastinum. No acute cardiopulmonary abnormality. A small or contained perforation is not excluded on plain film; CT is recommended if clinical concern persists.
handover.model:
• Read: erect film, adequate. No free subdiaphragmatic gas, no pneumomediastinum or surgical emphysema, clear lungs, no effusion.
  • Meaning: no radiographic evidence of a perforated ulcer or of oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave). Free gas is missed on a plain film in a proportion of perforations, so guarding still matters. Clear lungs are a useful baseline before fluid and transfusion in a 74-year-old.
  • Changes: surgical review now. If guarding or percussion tenderness persists after analgesia and resuscitation, CT abdomen with IV contrast before gastroscopy, because a perforation must be excluded before endoscopy.

ask: You are now calling the gastroenterology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Bruce Birkenstock, including your interpretation of these results and his Glasgow-Blatchford score.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Bruce now, here in the emergency department.
Bruce asks you, "What's caused this, and can I keep taking my tablets?" Answer him, including what he should call the nurse for, then tell me what you would ask the nurses to watch for.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Bruce Birkenstock, 74.
  • Situation: upper GI bleed with haematemesis and melaena, compensated hypovolaemia, Glasgow-Blatchford score 12 (13 on the repeat SBP); requesting gastroscopy within 24 hours.
  • Background: 2 weeks of melaena, 2 haematemeses today after sudden worsening of months of epigastric pain; ibuprofen 400 mg TDS and aspirin 100 mg, esomeprazole rarely taken; stroke 2013, hypertension; 2 to 3 drinks a day, no stigmata except one spider naevus.
  • Assessment: HR 112 rising to 116, SBP 110 falling to 106, further melaena; Hb 84 (baseline 138), urea 16.8, lactate 2.6; platelets, INR and LFTs normal apart from GGT, so likely non-variceal; erect CXR no free gas, but guarding.
  • Recommendation: two large-bore cannulas, crossmatch, fluid bolus and IV PPI started; please review for endoscopy, and I am asking surgery to see the guarding.

Non-variceal upper GI bleed from a peptic (probably duodenal) ulcer, NSAID and aspirin related: ibuprofen TDS plus aspirin, poor PPI adherence, nocturnal epigastric pain eased by food, haematemesis with melaena, Hb fall, urea 16.8.

  • Variceal bleeding (must not miss): for: alcohol, spider naevus, GGT; against: no other stigmata, normal platelets, INR, albumin and bilirubin.
  • Perforated ulcer (must not miss): for: sudden worse pain, guarding; against: soft abdomen, normal bowel sounds, no free gas.
  • Erosive oesophagitis or gastritis: for: GORD, missed PPI, NSAIDs, alcohol; against: bleed of this size.
  • Mallory-Weiss tear: against: no retching first, melaena for 2 weeks.
  • Gastric cancer: for: age; against: no weight loss or dysphagia.

1. Senior help, ABCDE: airway watch, anaesthetics early if further haematemesis or falling GCS; small crystalloid bolus (e.g. 500 mL) and reassess; early red cells (crossmatched or group-specific) if bleeding continues or no response; massive transfusion protocol if unstable.
  2. Restrictive transfusion: Hb below 70 g/L (below 80 g/L with significant cardiovascular disease, e.g. ischaemic heart disease), or ongoing instability; for Bruce, transfuse if not responding to the bolus; not to a normal Hb.
  3. Nil by mouth, IV PPI (e.g. pantoprazole 80 mg IV), titrated analgesia and antiemetic; no NSAIDs; no terlipressin, octreotide, antibiotics or tranexamic acid (non-variceal).
  4. Medications: stop ibuprofen permanently, withhold lisinopril; aspirin either continued or paused briefly and restarted within days once the bleeding is controlled, as decided with gastroenterology; not stopped indefinitely.
  5. GBS 12, admit with frequent observations and fluid balance; surgical review now, CT abdomen with IV contrast before gastroscopy if guarding persists; gastroscopy within 24 hours; HDU or ICU if unstable.

• Plain words: most likely an ulcer, a raw sore in the stomach or the first part of the bowel, caused by the anti-inflammatory tablets and aspirin; a camera test will find it and usually stop the bleeding.
  • Tablets: no more ibuprofen (paracetamol instead, GP to help with his arthritis); aspirin either continued or paused briefly and restarted within days once the bleeding is controlled, as decided with gastroenterology, to protect against stroke; take the stomach tablet every day.
  • Call the nurse at once: vomiting blood, black or bloody stool, feeling faint, worse pain.
  • Nurses: rising HR, falling BP, more bleeding, low urine output, confusion, rigid abdomen; clinical review for yellow zone, rapid response for red zone.

ddx.dx: Bleeding peptic ulcer (probably duodenal) related to NSAID and aspirin use
ddx.for: He takes ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with aspirin, rarely takes his PPI, has months of nocturnal epigastric pain eased by food, haematemesis with 2 weeks of melaena, a fall in Hb from 138 to 84 and a urea of 16.8.
He drinks 2 to 3 standard drinks a day, has a spider naevus on his chest and a mildly raised GGT.
ddx.against: Only one spider naevus with no other stigmata, no ascites or splenomegaly, and normal platelets, INR, albumin and bilirubin.

ddx.for: Sudden worsening of his epigastric pain with epigastric and right upper quadrant voluntary guarding and percussion tenderness.
ddx.against: The abdomen is soft and not distended with normal bowel sounds and no rigidity, and the erect chest X-ray shows no free gas.

ddx.dx: Severe erosive oesophagitis, gastritis or duodenitis
ddx.for: Long-standing GORD, missed esomeprazole, regular NSAIDs and daily alcohol.
ddx.against: Erosive disease rarely causes a bleed large enough to drop the Hb by more than 50 g/L with haemodynamic change.
There was no retching or vomiting before the blood, and the melaena started 2 weeks earlier.

ddx.for: He is 74 with months of epigastric pain and anaemia.
ddx.against: No weight loss, loss of appetite, dysphagia or early satiety.

guide:
In Part 1, Bruce answers the history, giving each detail only when he is asked. The examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. This is an acute station: credit the candidate who calls for senior help and asks for cannulas and a crossmatch early (item 3), then continues the focused history and examination. The nurse reports the further melaena partway through. If the candidate orders treatment in Part 1, the nurse confirms it and the examiner says "Noted, please cover it in Part 2". If they ask for postural observations, the nurse says they have not been done and he is on bed rest. Do not require postural observations; credit a candidate who says they are not needed or not safe because he already has a resting tachycardia. If they ask for results or imaging, say these will come in Part 2.

In Part 2, hand over the observations, the bloods and gas, and the erect chest X-ray report, then ask all four questions in order. Both observation sets were taken before any treatment had run in; if a bolus was ordered, say it is now running. Read out Bruce's question to open question 4; he asks his follow-up questions while the candidate answers.

Do not penalise a candidate who gives an IV PPI without a specific dose, or who names esomeprazole instead of pantoprazole. For aspirin, credit either continuing it or pausing it briefly with a plan to restart, if the decision is made with the team; do not credit stopping it with no plan to restart. Do not credit routine terlipressin, octreotide or antibiotics without a stated suspicion of varices, automatic transfusion to a "normal" Hb, or large-volume crystalloid.

A high-performing candidate gets help and access early, characterises both the haematemesis and the melaena, and asks about syncope. They find the ibuprofen, aspirin and missed PPI, quantify the alcohol and look for chronic liver disease. They pick up the guarding and ask for a rectal examination. In Part 2 they read the observations as compensated shock despite a white-zone chart, calculate a high Glasgow-Blatchford score, call the bleed non-variceal on the bloods, and say a clear erect film does not exclude perforation. They resuscitate with restrictive transfusion, give an IV PPI, stop the NSAID, make an explicit plan for the aspirin with the team, and arrange endoscopy within 24 hours.

A borderline candidate takes the history but misses the medication link or the alcohol, is reassured by "normal" observations, transfuses to a target without a threshold, or forgets the endoscopy and surgical review. A failing candidate does not escalate, or plans discharge.
explain:
Diagnosis: non-variceal upper GI bleed from a peptic ulcer

Upper GI bleeding comes from above the ligament of Treitz and still carries a substantial mortality, especially in older patients with comorbidities. Bruce has had melaena for 2 weeks and then two large haematemeses after a sudden worsening of months of epigastric pain. The pain woke him at night and eased with food, which is typical of a duodenal ulcer. His risk factors stack up: regular ibuprofen, daily aspirin, a PPI he rarely takes, and daily alcohol. Peptic ulcer disease is the commonest cause of upper GI bleeding. NSAIDs, aspirin and Helicobacter pylori are its main causes, and NSAIDs and aspirin together multiply the risk.

Three key decisions

  • Stable or unstable? Resuscitate before endoscopy. Bruce is tachycardic with a BP of 110/80, low for a man with hypertension, a CRT of 3 seconds, a raised lactate and ongoing melaena. He is in compensated hypovolaemic shock even though his chart is in the white zone. Older patients and those on antihypertensives compensate poorly and can decompensate suddenly.
  • Variceal or non-variceal? This changes the drugs and the thresholds. Look for stigmata of chronic liver disease, alcohol use, thrombocytopenia, a raised INR and low albumin. Bruce has one spider naevus, which can occur in healthy people, and otherwise normal results. His bleed is presumed non-variceal, so terlipressin, octreotide and prophylactic antibiotics are not given.
  • Major or minor? The Glasgow-Blatchford score predicts the need for intervention (transfusion, endoscopic therapy or surgery). A score of 0, or 1 in many protocols, identifies patients who may be managed as outpatients. Bruce scores 12: he is high risk and needs admission and early endoscopy.

History and examination

Ask about the volume and colour of the haematemesis (fresh blood or coffee grounds), the duration of melaena, syncope (it scores in the Glasgow-Blatchford score), cardiac symptoms, and whether retching came first (Mallory-Weiss). Ask specifically about NSAIDs, aspirin, other antiplatelets, anticoagulants, steroids and SSRIs, and about PPI adherence. Quantify alcohol and screen for liver disease and for malignancy (weight loss, dysphagia). Ask early whether the patient would accept blood products. A Jehovah's Witness patient may refuse some or all products, and this changes the plan.

Examine for pallor and perfusion, stigmata of chronic liver disease, and peritonism. Postural observations add nothing once there is a resting tachycardia, and standing a bleeding older patient risks syncope. Guarding raises perforation. Feel the aorta: an aortoenteric fistula is rare but lethal in patients with an aneurysm or a graft. A rectal examination confirms melaena; when a melaena stool has already been seen, it can be documented later with a chaperone. Maroon or fresh red blood PR with haemodynamic compromise would suggest a very brisk upper bleed and should prompt even more urgent endoscopy.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: trends matter more than single values. A rising HR, a falling SBP with an already narrow pulse pressure, ongoing melaena and a worried nurse all call for an urgent senior review. No urine has been passed yet, but after about 20 minutes in the ED this is not oliguria; an IDC is needed to measure output.
  • Haemoglobin: 84 g/L against a baseline of 138. The first Hb underestimates an acute bleed, because haemodilution takes hours. The normal MCV shows the loss is mainly recent.
  • White cells: a mild neutrophilia with a normal total WCC fits a stress response to acute haemorrhage, but with guarding it is another reason to keep a low threshold for CT.
  • Urea: 16.8 mmol/L with a near-normal creatinine. Blood digested in the gut is absorbed as protein, and hypovolaemia adds to it, which points to an upper source.
  • Liver and coagulation: normal platelets, INR, albumin and bilirubin argue against cirrhosis. The mild GGT rise fits his alcohol intake.
  • Lactate 2.6 mmol/L: tissue hypoperfusion.
  • Glasgow-Blatchford score: urea 10 to under 25 mmol/L (4), Hb below 100 g/L in a man (6), SBP 110 or more (0), HR 100 or more (1), melaena (1), no syncope, liver disease or cardiac failure: 12. With the repeat SBP of 106 it is 13.
  • Erect chest X-ray: requested because of the guarding. It shows no free gas, but a plain film misses some perforations, so CT abdomen with IV contrast is needed, before gastroscopy, if the signs persist after analgesia and resuscitation. Endoscopic insufflation into a perforation is dangerous.

Differentials

  • Peptic ulcer disease (gastric or duodenal).
  • Severe oesophagitis, gastritis or duodenitis.
  • Varices and portal hypertensive gastropathy.
  • Mallory-Weiss tear.
  • Angiodysplasia.
  • Upper GI malignancy.
  • Boerhaave syndrome (oesophageal rupture after forceful vomiting, often with chest pain and surgical emphysema). The clear chest film and the history make it unlikely here.

Management in the ED

  • Immediate: call for senior help and a rapid response if he deteriorates. Involve gastroenterology early, and general surgery, theatre and anaesthetics as needed.
    • A: patency and protection. Ongoing haematemesis or a falling conscious level may need intubation before endoscopy.
    • B: oxygen only if hypoxic.
    • C: two large-bore cannulas. Group and crossmatch, FBC, coagulation, UEC and LFTs. ECG (and troponin if chest pain or ECG changes) to look for demand ischaemia. A small crystalloid bolus with reassessment, avoiding over-resuscitation. Transfuse early if loss continues or he does not respond: group-specific or crossmatched red cells (his group is known), emergency group O red cells only if these are not immediately available, and the massive transfusion protocol if he becomes unstable.
    • D: BGL and temperature. Look for other bleeding sources.
    • Reassess continually with serial observations.
  • Once stable:
    • Regular observations, nil by mouth, an IDC and fluid balance.
    • A restrictive transfusion strategy: transfuse for Hb below 70 g/L, below 80 g/L with significant cardiovascular disease (e.g. ischaemic heart disease), or ongoing instability, rather than to a normal Hb. Liberal transfusion increases rebleeding and mortality in upper GI bleeding. For Bruce, have 2 units crossmatched and held in the blood bank ready to issue, and collect them only once the decision to transfuse is made: red cells should start within 30 minutes of leaving controlled storage and finish within 4 hours.
    • An IV PPI before endoscopy.
    • Titrated IV opioid analgesia (e.g. fentanyl 25–50 microg or morphine 2.5 mg IV increments, cautiously given his BP) and an IV antiemetic (e.g. ondansetron 4 mg IV); no NSAIDs. Re-examine the abdomen after analgesia to decide whether CT is needed.
    • No terlipressin, octreotide or antibiotics unless variceal bleeding is suspected. Tranexamic acid is not recommended: the HALT-IT trial showed no benefit and more venous thrombosis.
  • Medications: stop the ibuprofen for good and withhold lisinopril. Aspirin given for secondary prevention after stroke should not be stopped indefinitely: it is either continued or paused briefly and restarted within days (ideally within 3 to 5 days) once the bleeding is controlled, as decided with gastroenterology, because stopping it raises the risk of another cardiovascular or cerebrovascular event. Review the PPI and make it regular.
  • Definitive: urgent gastroscopy within 24 hours via gastroenterology, sooner if he is unstable, once a perforation has been excluded. The gastroscopy diagnoses the lesion, gives endoscopic haemostasis for high-risk features and takes biopsies for H. pylori. A negative H. pylori test during the acute bleed or on a PPI should be repeated later (for example a urea breath test off PPI, or serology). A high-dose PPI continues after endoscopic therapy. Interventional radiology or surgery is used if endoscopy fails.
  • Disposition: admit under gastroenterology or general medicine, with HDU or ICU if he is unstable.

Consent for transfusion

Explain which products may be needed: red cells, and occasionally FFP, platelets or cryoprecipitate. Explain why they are needed, and the risks: fever, rash, fluid overload (a real concern at 74), haemolytic and allergic reactions, and, very rarely in Australia, infection. Check for objections, especially in Jehovah's Witness patients, and document the consent.

Safety netting and follow-up

In hospital, Bruce and the nurses report further haematemesis, melaena, faintness, worsening pain or chest pain at once. The nurses escalate falling BP, a rising HR, low urine output, confusion or a rigid abdomen. On discharge he takes the PPI regularly, never restarts the NSAID (paracetamol for his arthritis), and completes H. pylori eradication if he tests positive. He follows the team's plan for his aspirin and has a GP review in 1 to 2 weeks for a repeat Hb, iron studies, his blood pressure and alcohol advice. He calls 000 or returns to the ED for black stools, vomiting blood or collapse.
points: In upper GI bleeding, decide three things early: stable or unstable, variceal or non-variceal, and major or minor (Glasgow-Blatchford score). Each changes the management.

A white-zone chart can hide compensated shock: tachycardia, a BP low for that patient, slow capillary refill, a raised lactate and ongoing melaena mean active bleeding, especially in older patients on antihypertensives.
The first Hb underestimates an acute bleed, and a urea raised out of proportion to creatinine points to an upper GI source.

Transfuse restrictively (Hb below 70 g/L, below 80 g/L with significant cardiovascular disease such as ischaemic heart disease, or ongoing instability). Give an IV PPI and arrange endoscopy within 24 hours. Give terlipressin, octreotide and antibiotics only for suspected varices, and do not give tranexamic acid.

NSAIDs and aspirin, especially together and without a PPI, are a major cause of peptic ulcer bleeding. Stop the NSAID for good. Aspirin given for secondary prevention is either continued or paused briefly and restarted within days once the bleeding is controlled, as decided with gastroenterology; it is not stopped indefinitely.
Guarding in a GI bleed raises perforation: an erect chest X-ray helps, but a clear film does not exclude it, and CT and surgical review follow before endoscopy if concern persists.
